Load configuration files
- location of model drivers, rds files (containing models), tables of parameter estimates and performance metrics, and figures. 
```{r}
read_properties <- function(file_path) {
  lines <- readLines(file_path)
  lines <- lines[grepl("=", lines)]  # only keep lines with key-value pairs
  key_vals <- strsplit(lines, "=")
  props <- setNames(
    trimws(sapply(key_vals, `[`, 2)),
    trimws(sapply(key_vals, `[`, 1))
  )
  return(props)
}
```

```{r}
df <- read.csv(file.path(drivers_root, "burned_area_jja_2002_2011_new.csv")) %>%
  dplyr::select(-starts_with("X"))

df <- df %>% mutate(
  road_proximity_binary  = if_else(dist_road  >= 30, 0, 1),
  urban_proximity_binary = if_else(dist_urban >= 40, 0, 1),
  river_proximity_binary = if_else(dist_river >= 30, 0, 1)
)
nrow(df)
df <- na.omit(df)
nrow(df)

# read in rows with fire count exceeding strike count and compare with burned area
null_rows <- read.csv(file.path(drivers_root, "null_ignition_rows_training_data_2002-2011.csv")) %>%
  dplyr::select(-X)

  dplyr::select(year, lat, lon, month, fire_count) %>%
  rename(fire_count_null = fire_count) %>%
  mutate(null_row = 1)

df_nulls <- df %>%
  full_join(null_rows, by = c("lon", "lat", "year", "month")) %>%
  mutate(null_row = replace_na(null_row, 0))

filter(df_nulls, null_row == 1) %>%
  group_by(year, month, lat, lon) %>%
  summarise(total_burned_area = sum(burned_area_km2_total), n_fires = n(), .groups = "drop")

#these null rows need to be dropped. 

df_nulls <- filter(df_nulls, null_row == 0) 
summary(df_nulls$burned_area_km2_total)

df <- df_nulls
```

# =============================================================================
Vapor pressure deficit (VPD), computed from tair (Kelvin) and rh (%),
using the standard FAO-56 Penman-Monteith / Tetens saturation-vapor-
pressure formula. Added directly to df, BEFORE the train/test split, so
it's available to every model downstream exactly like any other predictor.
# =============================================================================
```{r}


df <- df %>%
  mutate(
    tair_C = tair - 273.15,                                  # Kelvin -> Celsius
    es     = 0.6108 * exp((17.27 * tair_C) / (tair_C + 237.3)), # saturation vapor pressure, kPa
    ea     = es * (rh / 100),                                 # actual vapor pressure, kPa
    vpd    = es - ea                                          # vapor pressure deficit, kPa
  )

summary(df$vpd)   # sanity check -- should be non-negative, roughly 0-3 kPa for these conditions
```




Split into training and testing data
```{r, echo=FALSE}
## 80% of the sample size
sample_size <- floor(0.8 * nrow(df))

## set the seed to make partition reproducible
set.seed(123)
train_index <- sample(seq_len(nrow(df)), size = sample_size)

train <- df[train_index, ]
test <- df[-train_index, ]
```


```{r}
# ── Save scaling parameters ───────────────────────────────────────────────────
predictors_ignition <- c("rh", "tair", "precip", "wind", "vpd",
                          "precip_1m", "precip_2m", "precip_3m", "precip_5y",
                          "tair_1m", "tair_2", "tair_2m", "tair_5y", "B", "C", "U") 


mu_rh        <- mean(train$rh);        sigma_rh        <- sd(train$rh)
mu_tair      <- mean(train$tair);      sigma_tair      <- sd(train$tair)
mu_precip    <- mean(train$precip);    sigma_precip    <- sd(train$precip)
mu_wind      <- mean(train$wind);      sigma_wind      <- sd(train$wind)
mu_vpd      <- mean(train$vpd);      sigma_vpd      <- sd(train$vpd)
mu_precip_1m <- mean(train$precip_1m); sigma_precip_1m <- sd(train$precip_1m)
mu_precip_2m <- mean(train$precip_2m); sigma_precip_2m <- sd(train$precip_2m)
mu_precip_3m <- mean(train$precip_3m); sigma_precip_3m <- sd(train$precip_3m)
mu_precip_5y <- mean(train$precip_5y); sigma_precip_5y <- sd(train$precip_5y)
mu_tair_1m   <- mean(train$tair_1m);   sigma_tair_1m   <- sd(train$tair_1m)
mu_tair_2m   <- mean(train$tair_2m);   sigma_tair_2m   <- sd(train$tair_2m)
mu_tair_3m   <- mean(train$tair_3m);   sigma_tair_3m   <- sd(train$tair_3m)
mu_tair_5y   <- mean(train$tair_5y);   sigma_tair_5y   <- sd(train$tair_5y)
mu_B         <- mean(train$B);         sigma_B         <- sd(train$B)
mu_C         <- mean(train$C);         sigma_C         <- sd(train$C)
mu_U         <- mean(train$U);         sigma_U         <- sd(train$U)



# Store and save
mean_sd_ignition <- data.frame(
  var   = predictors_ignition,
  mu    = c(mu_rh, mu_tair, mu_precip, mu_wind, mu_vpd,
            mu_precip_1m, mu_precip_2m, mu_precip_3m, mu_precip_5y,
            mu_tair_1m, mu_tair_2m, mu_tair_3m, mu_tair_5y, mu_B, mu_C, mu_U),
            #mu_road_proximity_binary, mu_urban_proximity_binary, mu_river_proximity_binary),
  sigma = c(sigma_rh, sigma_tair, sigma_precip, sigma_wind, sigma_vpd,
            sigma_precip_1m, sigma_precip_2m, sigma_precip_3m, sigma_precip_5y,
            sigma_tair_1m, sigma_tair_2m, sigma_tair_3m, sigma_tair_5y, sigma_B, sigma_C, sigma_U))
            #sigma_road_proximity_binary, sigma_urban_proximity_binary, sigma_river_proximity_binary)


write.csv(mean_sd_ignition,
          file.path(mu_sigma_root, "mu_sigma_burned_area_predictors.csv"),
          row.names = FALSE)

# ── Standardize train ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
train <- train %>%
  mutate(
    rh        = (rh        - mu_rh)        / sigma_rh,
    tair      = (tair      - mu_tair)      / sigma_tair,
    precip    = (precip    - mu_precip)    / sigma_precip,
    wind      = (wind      - mu_wind)      / sigma_wind,
    vpd      = (vpd      - mu_vpd)      / sigma_vpd,

    B         = (B         - mu_B)         / sigma_B,
```

With such large spread in fire size, a mixture model is worth testing: classifier decides whether this will be an extremem fire size or typical, based on a 95% threshold (fire size above the 95th percentile is labeled extreme). Then, two separate gamma bayes models are fit for extreme versusu typical fire sizes.. First, look at predictors that will be best suited for each submodel. 

Classifier model - which predictors are good at catching whether a fire will be classified as extreme or typical?
```{r}
library(dplyr)
library(tidyr)
library(ggplot2)

# ── Define "large fire" threshold ──────────────────────────────────────────
# Using top 5% of burned area as the "extreme" group; adjust as needed
threshold <- quantile(train$burned_area_km2_total, 0.95)
train <- train %>%
  mutate(is_extreme = as.integer(burned_area_km2_total >= threshold))

cat(sprintf("Threshold (95th pct): %.2f km2\n", threshold))
cat(sprintf("N extreme fires: %d / %d (%.1f%%)\n",
            sum(train$is_extreme), nrow(train), 100 * mean(train$is_extreme)))

# ── 1. Univariate comparison: does each predictor differ between groups? ──
predictors <- c("rh", "tair", "precip", "wind", "vpd",
                "precip_1m", "precip_3m", "precip_5y",
                "tair_2m", "tair_5y", "C", "U", "urban_proximity_binary")

univariate_tests <- lapply(predictors, function(v) {
  x_extreme <- train[[v]][train$is_extreme == 1]
  x_normal  <- train[[v]][train$is_extreme == 0]

  # Wilcoxon rank-sum test — robust to non-normality, appropriate given
  # your predictors are already standardised but likely non-normal within group
  wt <- tryCatch(wilcox.test(x_extreme, x_normal), error = function(e) NULL)

  data.frame(
    predictor    = v,
    mean_extreme = mean(x_extreme, na.rm = TRUE),
    mean_normal  = mean(x_normal, na.rm = TRUE),
    diff         = mean(x_extreme, na.rm = TRUE) - mean(x_normal, na.rm = TRUE),
    p_value      = if (!is.null(wt)) wt$p.value else NA_real_
  )
})

univariate_results <- do.call(rbind, univariate_tests) %>%
  arrange(p_value)

print(univariate_results)

# ── 2. Visualize: boxplots of each predictor by extreme/normal ────────────
train_long <- train %>%
  dplyr::select(all_of(predictors), is_extreme) %>%
  pivot_longer(-is_extreme, names_to = "predictor", values_to = "value")

ggplot(train_long, aes(x = factor(is_extreme), y = value)) +
  geom_boxplot(outlier.size = 0.5) +
  facet_wrap(~predictor, scales = "free_y") +
  labs(x = "Extreme fire (1 = top 5% burned area)", y = "Standardised value") +
  theme_minimal()

# ── 3. Multivariate check: can predictors jointly classify extreme fires? ──
# A quick random forest AUC tells you the *ceiling* on how separable the
# groups are given these predictors, independent of the burned-area model
library(randomForest)
library(pROC)

set.seed(123)
rf_data <- train %>% dplyr::select(all_of(predictors), is_extreme) %>%
  mutate(is_extreme = factor(is_extreme))

rf_fit <- randomForest(is_extreme ~ ., data = rf_data, ntree = 500,
                        importance = TRUE)

rf_probs <- predict(rf_fit, type = "prob")[, "1"]
rf_auc   <- auc(roc(rf_data$is_extreme, rf_probs, quiet = TRUE))
cat(sprintf("\nRandom forest AUC for separating extreme fires: %.3f\n", rf_auc))

# Variable importance — which predictors carry the most separating signal
importance_df <- as.data.frame(importance(rf_fit)) %>%
  tibble::rownames_to_column("predictor") %>%
  arrange(desc(MeanDecreaseGini))

print(importance_df)
```

worth keeping: urban_proximity_binary (p = 6.6e-13), rh (p = 3.6e-9), tair (p = 9.3e-8), precip (p = 1.75e-4), tair_5y (p = 8.95e-4)
Borderline: precip_3m, precip_1m (p ≈ 0.02–0.03)


What about fires below the 0.95 threshold? What predictors will do well at estimating smaller fire sizes?
```{r}

typical_only <- train %>%
  filter(burned_area_km2_total < threshold)

predictors_all <- c("rh", "tair", "precip", "wind", "vpd", "precip_1m", "precip_3m",
                     "precip_5y", "tair_2m", "tair_5y", "C", "U", "urban_proximity_binary")

within_typical_cor <- sapply(predictors_all, function(v) {
  cor(typical_only[[v]], log(typical_only$burned_area_km2_total), use = "complete.obs")
})

sort(within_typical_cor, decreasing = TRUE)
```
Highes correlation: "urban_proximity_binary", "tair_2m", "tair". RH might be worth including (-0.119), since its opposing negative correlation compared with lightning and ignition models will encourage contraditory outcomes between fire count and size (ie. many small fires)

among typical (non-extreme) fires, monthly climate variables explain very little of the variation in burned area on their own.This is consistent with and helps explain the persistently negative R² I keep seeing across every model variant in this whole script (below) It's not that the models are poorly specified, it's that the typical-fire regime may genuinely be close to climate-independent at this temporal/spatial resolution, with size instead driven by factors you don't have in this dataset (fine-scale fuel continuity, suppression response timing, terrain).

And now, extremem fires - what predictors are better fit to predict extreme fires?
```{r}

extreme_only <- train %>%
  filter(burned_area_km2_total > threshold)

predictors_all <- c("rh", "tair", "precip", "wind", "vpd", "precip_1m", "precip_3m",
                     "precip_5y", "tair_2m", "tair_5y", "C", "U", "urban_proximity_binary")

within_extreme_cor <- sapply(predictors_all, function(v) {
  cor(extreme_only[[v]], log(extreme_only$burned_area_km2_total), use = "complete.obs")
})

sort(within_extreme_cor, decreasing = TRUE)
```
U is strongest (0.339), then precip_3m (-0.30384388), precip_5y (-0.28054696), C (-0.27449596), and tair (0.23708349)
Interesting that urban proximity drops!
May be worth again including RH (-0.25135813) since its influece on burned area is opposite to fire count.

# ---- Check for colinearity between predictors --- 

Condition number (kappa(X)) is a diagnostic metric that assesses the severity of multicollinearity across the entire set of predictors. It measures how unstable or sensitive your model's coefficient estimates are to tiny changes in the data.

1 to 10 (Low Collinearity): The predictors are nearly orthogonal (independent). The model is numerically stable, and coefficients are reliable.
10 to 30 (Moderate Collinearity): Interdependence is present. The variance of your coefficients is inflating, but it may not destroy the model's predictive power.
Greater than 30 (Severe Collinearity): Strong linear dependencies exist. Minor tweaks to your data will cause massive, erratic swings in your coefficient signs and values

```{r}
preds <- c("rh", "tair", "precip", "wind", "vpd",
                          "precip_1m", "precip_2m","precip_3m","precip_5y",
                          "tair_1m", "tair_2m", "tair_3m", "tair_5y", "C", "U",
                         "road_proximity_binary", "urban_proximity_binary")

X <- model.matrix(as.formula(paste("~", paste(preds, collapse = " + "))),
                  data = train)
kappa(X)   # values > 1e6 (1,000,000) indicate severe collinearity
cor(train[, preds])  # look for correlations > 0.9

cor(train[, preds])> 0.9  # look for correlations > 0.9
```
Correlation results:
precip_2m and precip_3m: r = 0.937 — this is the problematic correlation. These two variables are carrying nearly identical information, which will destabilize the GLM fitting algorithm. remove precip_2m (between 1m and 3m). precip_1m captures very recent fuel moisture (FFMC/DMC analogue) and precip_3m captures the longer-term moisture deficit (DC analogue). The middle lag is redundant given those two endpoints are included.

tair_1m, 2m, 3m: r >0.9. remove tair_1m and tair_3m

Proximity data, r>0.9. random forest identifies road as having lower importance - remove.

B, C, U all sum to 1, also introducing autocorrelation - remove B, lowest of the three in importance according to the random forest. 

##########################
Explore interaction terms:
##########################
- humidity's suppressing effect (negative correlation) on extreme-fire probability is itself different in urban-proximate vs. remote areas (e.g., suppression resources mean humidity matters less near infrastructure, since fires get controlled early regardless), that's a physically sensible interaction and directly testable with the LRT approach

- U x rh: U (land cover fraction) is consistently one of your strongest extreme-fire-size predictors; whether more fuel amplifies or dampens the effect of dryness on fire size is a classic fire-behavior interaction (more fuel + dry conditions compounding, vs. fuel-limited growth regardless of dryness)

This test only looks at the classifier - is the fire extrme or not?
```{r}
library(iml)
rf_data_features_only <- rf_data %>% dplyr::select(-is_extreme)

predictor <- Predictor$new(rf_fit, data = rf_data_features_only, y = rf_data$is_extreme)
interact <- Interaction$new(predictor, feature = "rh")
plot(interact)

```
H-statistic: urban_proximity_binary:rh (≈0.92), U:rh (≈0.90), and vpd:rh (≈0.87) are the top three

Plot: bin one continuous predictor into terciles (3 equal quantiles), then plot the outcome against the other predictor, colored/faceted by that tercile:
```{r}
train %>%
  mutate(var_tercile = ntile(vpd, 3)) %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = rh, y = log(burned_area_km2_total + 1), color = factor(var_tercile))) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.4) +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", se = FALSE) +
  labs(color = "vpd tercile")

train %>%
  mutate(var_tercile = ntile(urban_proximity_binary, 2)) %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = rh, y = log(burned_area_km2_total + 1), color = factor(var_tercile))) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.4) +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", se = FALSE) +
  labs(color = "urban_proximity_binary tercile")

train %>%
  mutate(var_tercile = ntile(U, 3)) %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = rh, y = log(burned_area_km2_total + 1), color = factor(var_tercile))) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.4) +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", se = FALSE) +
  labs(color = "U tercile")
```
All three plots show visibly different slopes across terciles — vpd tercile 3 (high VPD, blue) is nearly flat with a high intercept, while tercile 1 (red) drops off steeply; U shows the most dramatic split, with tercile 1 (low openland) essentially flat while terciles 2–3 fall off sharply; urban_proximity_binary shows a real but more modest difference between its two groups.

Likelihood-ratio test via a quick frequentist GLM as a quick screen. Fit the same classifier/magnitude equation as a plain glm(), once without an interaction and once with it, and compare. 

Random forest resutls without intercations: urban_proximity_binary (p = 6.6e-13), rh (p = 3.6e-9), tair (p = 9.3e-8), precip (p = 1.75e-4), tair_5y (p = 8.95e-4)
```{r}
# no interactions, using predictors identified by the non interaction random forest
glm_main <- glm(is_extreme ~ urban_proximity_binary + rh + tair + precip + tair_5y,
                 data = train, family = binomial)

# use only interaction terms identified by interaction random forest
glm_interact <- glm(is_extreme ~ rh * urban_proximity_binary + rh * U + rh * vpd,
                     data = train, family = binomial)

#a blend of both
glm_both <- glm(is_extreme ~ rh * urban_proximity_binary + rh * U + rh * vpd + tair + precip + tair_5y,
                     data = train, family = binomial)


glm_limited_2 <- glm(is_extreme ~ rh * urban_proximity_binary + rh * U + rh * vpd + tair_5y,
                     data = train, family = binomial)

glm_limited_3 <- glm(is_extreme ~ rh : urban_proximity_binary + rh : U + rh : vpd + rh + U + tair_5y,
                     data = train, family = binomial)
```

The interaction itself never reaches conventional significance in any model you tested. In glm_4, wind:rh has p = 0.130; in glm_6 (the marginality-violating version, which tends to inflate an interaction's apparent significance by absorbing the main effect into it), it only gets to p = 0.059

Having said that, a bayes model will better handle the small sample size by allowing uncertainty in the posterior estimate. keep wind:rh interaction for now.

What distribution should I choose for the extreme fires. At the 95% threhold, the extreme fires look gamma-distributied. But at a 175 km2 burned area cutoff, the shape of the data changes a little. 

1. Use a mean residual life (mean excess) plot, the first tool. For a true GPD tail, E[X − u | X > u] should be roughly linear in u once you're above the correct threshold. Below the correct threshold, the line will bend/curve.
2. Parameter stability plot. Fit a GPD at many different candidate thresholds and plot how the estimated shape (ξ) and modified scale parameters change. If ξ is roughly stable (flat, within CI bands of each other) above some threshold but jumps around below it, that's strong, direct evidence for exactly where the tail "truly" begins — this is the most standard, defensible way to formally answer "where does the shape change" rather than eyeballing histograms.
```{r}
library(ismev)
mrl.plot(train$burned_area_km2_total, umin = 50, umax = 500)

gpd.fitrange(train$burned_area_km2_total, umin = 50, umax = 500, nint = 20)
```

Compare a GDP distribution fit to extreme burned areas versus a gamma distribution. Lower AIC is better. 
Start with the threshold set based on the 95% threshold - fires that make up the top 5% 
```{r}
#library(MASS)
ba_threshold <- 254.2795 #basaed on 95% threshold
# Fit GPD at your candidate threshold
gpd_fit <- gpd.fit(train$burned_area_km2_total, threshold = ba_threshold)
gpd.diag(gpd_fit)   # QQ-plot, return-level plot -- visual goodness-of-fit
if (xi_hat < 0) {
  implied_max <- ba_threshold - sigma_hat / xi_hat
  cat(sprintf("GPD-implied maximum burned area: %.1f km\u00b2 (observed max: %.1f km\u00b2)\n",
              implied_max, max(train$burned_area_km2_total)))
}

# Compare against a Gamma fit on the same exceedances via AIC, same
# principle as everything you've been doing with the GLM screens
exceedances <- train$burned_area_km2_total[train$burned_area_km2_total >= ba_threshold]
gamma_fit <- fitdistr(exceedances - ba_threshold + 0.001, "gamma")  # MASS::fitdistr
# Compare AIC: whichever is lower is the better-supported tail model AT THAT THRESHOLD
#AIC(gpd_fit) doesnt work on this class. use:
k_gpd <- length(gpd_fit$mle)   # number of estimated parameters (2: sigma, xi)
aic_gpd <- 2 * k_gpd + 2 * gpd_fit$nllh
aic_gpd 
AIC(gamma_fit)
```

Now set a threshold based on what I saw in the histogram, where a different shape appears when looking at fires greater than 175 km2. 

```{r}
library(evd)  # for dgpd()

ba_threshold <- 254.2795  # or whichever threshold you're testing
exceedances <- train$burned_area_km2_total[train$burned_area_km2_total >= ba_threshold] - ba_threshold

gpd_fit <- gpd.fit(train$burned_area_km2_total, threshold = ba_threshold)
sigma_hat <- gpd_fit$mle[1]
xi_hat    <- gpd_fit$mle[2]

cat(sprintf("Fitted GPD: sigma (scale) = %.2f, xi (shape) = %.3f\n", sigma_hat, xi_hat))

# Overlay fitted density on a histogram of the exceedances
x_seq <- seq(0, max(exceedances), length.out = 200)
gpd_density <- dgpd(x_seq, loc = 0, scale = sigma_hat, shape = xi_hat)

hist(exceedances, breaks = 15, freq = FALSE,
     main = sprintf("GPD fit at threshold = %f", ba_threshold),
     xlab = "Exceedance (burned area - threshold, km\u00b2)")
lines(x_seq, gpd_density, col = "steelblue", lwd = 2)
```
